A novel deep learning approach is introduced in this study to enhance the semantic communication system by extracting meaningful features from images and mapping them to text. The proposed solution utilizes a convolutional neural network (CNN) to analyze image pixels and a recurrent neural network (RNN) to translate features into words. Experimental results demonstrate that the system can effectively transmit text over a channel with minimal loss of accuracy, achieving an average word error rate of 0.03.

In the era of big data, analytics play a crucial role, but the increasing size of datasets and the complexity of real-time applications necessitate optimized results from these analytics to be applicable in practical settings. To address this, result-aware approaches focus on enhancing the efficiency of results from various analytics, encompassing data processing, storage, transmission, and retrieval phases. This paper presents a comprehensive survey of the latest result-aware big data analytics techniques, encompassing results from multiple data sources, including text, image, and video data. The study delves into the technical frameworks of result-aware analytics, their applications in real-world scenarios, and evaluates the current research, identifying potential challenges and future research directions in this field.

The 2-category of doctrines, denoted as Dtn, is examined with a focus on its modal operators. It is found that the concept of modal operators within Dtn is equivalent to the notion of a factorization of a doctrine D through the inclusion of a sub-doctrine D0, known as the base doctrine. Furthermore, this factorization is categorized into three types, referred to as modal interior, modal equivalence, and modal equivalence interior operators. It is discovered that the modal operators within Dtn can be represented through the use of sub-doctrine inclusions, which enables the construction of a factorization of a doctrine D by a sub-doctrine D0. This factorization is used to define the concept of modal operators within Dtn, which is found to be a factorization of D through the sub-doctrine D0. This result is applied to the construction of various doctrines, which are found to be instances of the factorization of a doctrine D by a sub-doctrine D0. This result is used to demonstrate the existence of various doctrines, which are found to be instances of the factorization of a doctrine D by a sub-doctrine D0. This result is used to demonstrate the existence of various doctrines, which are found to be instances of the factorization of a doctrine D by a sub-doctrine D0. This result is used to demonstrate the existence of various doctrines, which are found to be instances of the factorization of a doctrine D by a sub-doctrine

This study introduces a novel Bayesian approach for analyzing high-dimensional time series data with a focus on network modeling. The proposed method, a grouped Bayesian autoregression model, enables simultaneous network analysis and prediction of time series data. It incorporates a non-linear network model, a time-varying error structure, and a grouped autoregression model, with grouped autoregression coefficients sampled from a hierarchical Bayesian model. The grouped autoregression model's coefficients are estimated using a Gibbs sampling algorithm, and the Bayesian network structure is inferred using a Gibbs sampling algorithm within the grouped autoregression model. The method is applied to simulated data and a real-world dataset of daily stock returns to demonstrate its effectiveness.

The overwhelming amount of scientific information available makes it difficult for researchers to identify and verify the accuracy of scientific claims. This task is further complicated by the fact that most existing methods are not designed to handle the temporal and causal aspects of scientific knowledge. To address this issue, we introduce a new framework that extracts and evaluates the validity of scientific knowledge by analyzing the relationships between relevant variables over time. This framework, called SciKD, consists of two main components: a knowledge graph that captures the connections between variables and a neural network that assesses the direction of causality. By analyzing the knowledge graph and making predictions about the variables, SciKD can generate causal hypotheses that are then verified through a process of induction. We tested our framework on a large dataset of scientific claims and found that it outperformed other methods in identifying accurate causal relationships.

A novel, deep learning technique is developed to automatically segment the key compartments of the human eye, including the cornea, vitreous, and macula, using optical coherence tomography (OCT) scans. The proposed method leverages a U-Net architecture, paired with a convolutional encoder-decoder, to enhance its ability to accurately process and render detailed, multi-scale representations of the eye's structures. The technique is trained using a large dataset of 1000 retinal scans and 10,000 corresponding annotations, before being evaluated for its effectiveness through both qualitative and quantitative assessments. The results demonstrate the technique's ability to accurately identify the boundaries of the eye's structures, with a high degree of precision and recall, and outperform a comparable baseline method in terms of speed and accuracy.

Our approach involves incorporating a temporal element into cognitive modeling by
tracking the dynamic evolution of cognitive states over time. This is achieved through
the development of a neural network architecture, referred to as the Temporal Cognitive
Graph Network (TeCGN), which learns to dynamically update our existing model, CogTrans.
The Temporal Cognitive Graph, or TempCogn, serves as a learned temporal repository
that stores the evolution of cognitive states, with the TeCGN leveraging this structure
to dynamically adjust the CogTrans model based on the temporal context. This TempCogn
temporal repository is updated in real-time, allowing the model to adapt to new
information and past experiences. This dynamic learning approach is demonstrated
through experiments in a visual reasoning task, where the model's performance is
evaluated across varying time frames.

A well-known theorem has been proven to identify the exact number of Mersenne primes with specific characteristics, known as the Eight Levels Theorem. Building upon this concept, researchers have developed a new, more comprehensive approach called the Rank Eight Theorem, which provides a detailed understanding of Mersenne primes with larger exponents. This expanded theory is based on a new concept called rank, which is a measure of prime number properties. The theorem accurately categorizes Mersenne primes into distinct groups, each with unique characteristics, and provides a detailed understanding of these properties. This new approach has significant implications for the study of prime numbers and their properties.

The Boltzmann equation has been a subject of extensive research, particularly in regards to its ability to be reduced to hydrodynamic equations. Despite its importance, deriving the correct hydrodynamics from the Boltzmann equation remains a challenging task, largely due to the complexity of its relaxation dynamics. This paper presents a new approach to derive the hydrodynamics of the Boltzmann equation using the concept of entropy dissipation. A simplified model is first proposed to describe the relaxation process, which is then rigorously proven to lead to the Navier-Stokes shock structure and boundary layers. This model is found to be consistent with the Bénard equation under specific conditions. Moreover, it is demonstrated that the relaxation dynamics can be characterized by the concept of entropy dissipation, which is also applicable to other relaxation processes.

We have conducted a comprehensive study of a galaxy at redshift 6 using ALMA's high-resolution observations of CO and CN lines. We have made the first-ever detection of the CN molecule at redshift 6, and our analysis of the CO lines indicates that they are excited in a non-LTE state, which is consistent with the CN lines. We have used this information to estimate the temperature of the gas in this galaxy, which is approximately 80 Kelvin. We have also used ALMA's high-resolution capabilities to study the distribution of CO and CN in this galaxy, and our analysis suggests that the CN lines are a reliable indicator of the gas temperature. We have used this information to study the chemical properties of the galaxy, and our analysis suggests that the gas is primarily composed of hydrogen, with some carbon and nitrogen present. We have also used ALMA's high-resolution capabilities to study the distribution of CO and CN in this galaxy, and our analysis suggests that the gas is highly turbulent, with some regions having turbulent velocities of over 100 kilometers per second.

We introduce a novel dataset consisting of 3,000 sentences that have been annotated for 12 distinct task types. This diverse dataset is comprised of 1,500 English and 1,500 Spanish sentences, with each group further divided into sub-sets of 750 sentences each that exhibit varying levels of code-switching complexity. This unique dataset is a valuable resource for both research and teaching purposes, as it is well-suited for use in both NLP research and as a teaching resource for students studying computational linguistics. This work is a pioneering effort in providing annotated data for the language pair English-Spanish, particularly in the context of low-resource languages and code-switching.

The circumstellar discs of young stars are crucial for understanding how planets form and evolve. However, their properties are still not well understood, particularly in terms of how they lose mass. This study used data from the Chandra X-ray Observatory to investigate how X-ray radiation from young stars affects the mass-loss rates of their discs. The team analyzed data from 15 young stars and found that the discs of stars emitting more X-rays have higher mass-loss rates. This study also found a correlation between X-ray radiation and disc instability, suggesting that X-ray radiation could be the cause of this instability. The team's findings suggest that X-ray radiation from young stars can have a significant impact on their discs, particularly in terms of mass loss and instability.

A family of high-order, explicit generalized-$\alpha$ methods for hyperbolic problems is developed, where the methods' coefficients are determined by a diagonalization process applied to a matrix of Fourier modes, offering a unique, non-iterative approach to derive optimal coefficients. This work builds upon the generalized-$\alpha$ method and provides a new class of methods with improved stability and accuracy, including support for non-homogeneous boundary conditions. Numerical experiments are conducted to validate the enhanced stability and accuracy of these methods compared to existing techniques.

We have developed a comprehensive approach to study the behavior of a polaron in a bosonic environment using the non-equilibrium dynamical renormalization group method. Our study reveals that the polaron's residue exhibits a significant decrease as the coupling between the impurity and the bath increases, consistent with the concept of quasiparticle decay. Notably, the polaron's motion is constrained by the increasing mass due to the interaction with bosons, as evidenced by the rise in the polaron's effective mass. Our findings also show that the polaron's behavior is characterized by a non-monotonic temperature dependence, with a peak in the polaron's effective mass observed at intermediate temperatures.

The devastating impact of natural disasters like hurricanes on human life and property is heartbreaking, and providing necessary relief can be a significant challenge. To optimize the distribution of essential relief supplies such as food, water, and shelter, it's crucial to accurately determine the demand for these items. In this study, we develop a sophisticated model to forecast the demand for relief items following a hurricane landing in the Gulf Coast region of the United States. To achieve this, we utilize a combination of machine learning and natural language processing techniques to extract essential information from extensive social media data, including 1.3 million tweets generated during Hurricane Harvey. By integrating these tweets with existing datasets, we create a comprehensive dataset that incorporates demographic information, relief supply distribution statistics, and geospatial data, marking it as a pioneering open dataset in the field.

The gravitational waves produced by supermassive black hole binaries are a key area of research in gravitational wave astronomy, specifically in the area of pulsar timing arrays. To accurately analyze these gravitational waves, scientists use a complex method called the discrete Fourier transform. This approach is computationally expensive and can be a major constraint for large-scale data analysis. To overcome this issue, a new, more efficient method called the fast Fourier transform has been developed. This technique significantly reduces the processing time required for gravitational wave analysis. In this study, the performance of the discrete Fourier transform and the fast Fourier transform is compared in the context of gravitational wave analysis. The results show that the fast Fourier transform outperforms the discrete Fourier transform in terms of speed. This improvement in processing time is crucial for large-scale gravitational wave analysis.

In Bayesian coordination games with multiple equilibria, we examine how the uniqueness of equilibria is affected by the quality of private information each player has about the payoffs of their own actions. This private information is represented by the variance of their posterior distributions. We show that increasing this information quality does not necessarily make the equilibrium unique, but rather, we identify a specific range of values that could lead to a unique equilibrium. This range depends on the structure of the game, the number of players, and the number of equilibria in the original game. Our findings indicate that increasing the precision of private observations does not always improve coordination, but rather, we find that increasing the precision of private observations can sometimes make coordination more difficult in certain cases.

The terahertz spectroscopy technique has become a crucial tool in characterizing materials, but it is often hindered by the presence of water, especially in biological samples. Our study focuses on understanding how water affects terahertz measurements in aqueous solutions, revealing a complex relationship between concentration, temperature, and terahertz absorption. By analyzing the absorption properties of these solutions, we propose a method to correct for the terahertz signal distortion caused by water and demonstrate its effectiveness in accurately determining the optical properties of dry substances.

The COVID-19 pandemic has underscored the importance of developing AI-powered tools to assess and mitigate various risks. In this study, we utilize a novel approach to create a predictive model for identifying COVID-19 cases in the Republic of Ireland. Leveraging a combination of temporal and spatial data, our model employs a dynamic algorithm to segment and weight regions of interest, thereby generating a temporal-spatial weight map that informs our model's predictive output.

A novel, multi-resolution method for studying fluid-structure interactions has been developed, combining a high-resolution, multi-scale smoothed particle hydrodynamics approach with a continuum-based model for solid deformation. This new technique enables the coexistence of two different methods within a shared domain, allowing for a high level of accuracy and flexibility in modeling complex fluid-structure interactions. Through a series of numerical experiments, the effectiveness and advantages of this method have been demonstrated, particularly its ability to precisely capture the dynamics of solid objects and its capacity for efficiently integrating different numerical methods.

Topological insulators are characterized by unique properties resulting from topological ordering in their band structure, leading to novel transport behaviors. Specifically, the surface and edge of 3D topological insulators support helical states, which are protected against backscattering due to time-reversal symmetry. This results in the presence of the quantum spin Hall effect, where the surface conductivity exhibits a specific, integer value. In this research, the transport properties of a helical topological insulator's surface are investigated, employing a model that incorporates disorder and a magnetic field. The study reveals that the combination of disorder and a magnetic field gives rise to a quantized, hysteresis-free resistance plateau at a specific magnetic field. This plateau corresponds to a specific spin polarization state, which is protected by the presence of the magnetic field. The research further shows that the plateau remains stable even in the presence of disorder, which is attributed to a mechanism of disorder-induced symmetry that prevents backscattering. The study also demonstrates that the resistance plateau can be controlled by adjusting the strength of the magnetic field. The findings of this research open up a new area of research in topological insulators, which involves the combination of disorder and a magnetic field to control the transport properties of a topological insulator's surface.

The HEP Software Foundation's Physics Event Generator Working Group has created a draft plan outlining its structure and focus areas. This plan was submitted as part of the HL-LHC review process, with input sought from relevant individuals and groups by the working group's co-leads. This initial document will be refined based on the feedback received, with a final version to be submitted to the HERINC conference in June 2021.

We examine properties of certain transformations on high-dimensional spaces that have specific characteristics, and show that under certain conditions, they can be used to create uniform measures. This involves demonstrating the absence of certain repeating patterns associated with these transformations, and in doing so, we identify a class of mappings that can be seen as variations of a basic model, similar to how this can be done with random processes.

Using the Green Bank Telescope, we conducted a comprehensive search for OH and H$_2$O emission in the outer Galaxy (R $>$ 90 km s$^{-1}$) and found thermal OH emission extending up to 2 kpc from the Galactic center. This discovery reveals a previously unknown structure of molecular gas in the outer Galaxy, which is not detected through CO emission. The OH emission is characterized by a distinct structure, with a central peak and two distinct wings, suggesting a spiral arm-like configuration. The observed structure is consistent with a model of a barred spiral galaxy, with a central bar and two spiral arms, which is supported by the distribution of CO emission. The OH emission is not associated with H$_2$O emission, which is more confined to the central regions. The OH emission is also found to be more prominent in the first and second quads, which is also observed in the HI gas. The observed structure is consistent with a model of a barred spiral galaxy, with a central bar and two spiral arms, which is supported by the distribution of CO emission. The OH emission is also found to be more prominent in the first and second quads, which is also observed in the HI gas. This research examines a consumer-driven economy, where consumers have diverse preferences for labor and goods, influencing the formation of labor markets. We use a general model to study a two-period economy, analyzing the short-term and long-term effects of consumer preferences and consumer mortality rates. Our findings indicate that a unique equilibrium exists in the short term but multiple equilibria exist in the long term. We discover that consumer preferences can impact wage levels and consumer welfare, leading to a situation where improving preferences may not necessarily improve welfare. We also explore the relationship between consumer mortality rates and consumer spending, showing that a moderate increase in mortality can lead to a decline in spending despite stable preferences, even if other factors remain constant.

We investigate the behavior of a two-dimensional system comprising polar, active particles that repel each other and are driven by random noise. Our findings indicate that the system undergoes a second-order phase transition, exhibiting polar order, in contrast to the complete disorder of particles. The characteristics of this transition are analyzed through the behavior of correlation functions and structure factors, and we identify the associated scaling exponents. Furthermore, we examine the impact of activity on this transition, and our results are compared to simulations that demonstrate the influence of varying parameters.

The decay process involving the transition of the $\Xi_{cc}^{++}$ baryon into a $\Xi_c^+$ baryon and a lepton-antilepton pair is examined within the framework of light-cone quantum chromodynamics. The transition form factors for this process are calculated, and the decay width is determined to be approximately $1.08$ keV, with a notable dependence on the form factor $S(t)$ that peaks at a specific value of $t$. The predicted decay width is then compared to the threshold where the $\Xi_{cc}^+$ baryon decays into the $\Xi_c^+$ baryon and a leron-antileton pair.

This paper explores a cooperative localization problem, where a group of agents, known as Observers, use their own measurements and those from a single Agent, called the Locator, to estimate the Locator's position. The Locator's task is to provide its current estimate to the Observers, who then update their estimates based on both the Locator's estimate and their own measurements. The process is repeated iteratively. We develop a novel algorithm, called the Iterative Localization (IL) method, based on the Kalman Filter, to solve this cooperative localization problem. Theoretical analysis confirms the algorithm's stability, and simulations demonstrate its effectiveness compared to existing methods, especially in scenarios with limited Observers.

This paper presents a novel approach to diagnosing faults in rotating machinery using band filters and the K-means clustering algorithm. The method aims to pinpoint specific frequency bands containing useful information for fault detection and classification, which is then utilized for feature extraction. A custom metric, the Band Relevance Factor (BRF), is introduced to determine the most relevant frequency bands. Unlike conventional band filter techniques, this method leverages the K-means algorithm to pinpoint optimal band combinations, effectively eliminating the need for manual tuning. The proposed method's effectiveness is demonstrated through a comparative study involving a simulated gearbox with tooth breakage, demonstrating improved performance when compared to other methods.

The study of CaTSi3 (where T = Pt and Ir) superconductors, utilizing muon spectroscopy and neutron diffraction, has been conducted to examine their internal crystal structure and superconducting properties. The analysis of muon spin rotation and zero-field time-of-flight spectra on CaPtSi3 and CaIrSi3 at temperatures below their superconducting transition points reveals a preserved time-reversal symmetry. The obtained results are consistent with the calculated density functional theory predictions, indicating that these materials possess a noncentrosymmetric structure. The neutron diffraction data further confirms the noncentrosymmetric nature of these compounds. The observed superconductivity in these materials is likely to be the first instance of noncentrosymmetric superconductivity.

This paper presents a novel approach to solving optimal control problems in high-dimensional nonconvex settings using sparse grid techniques. The proposed method employs a two-grid method, leveraging a sparse grid for the source term and a dense grid for the cost function, to achieve efficient computation. The approach is grounded in the maximum principle and utilizes the classical optimality conditions for nonlinear programming, with numerical simulations demonstrating the efficacy of the sparse grid method. Notably, the proposed algorithm exhibits a superlinear convergence rate, and preliminary numerical results indicate that it outperforms the two-grid method in terms of computational time, particularly for large sparse grids.

A novel approach is introduced for density estimation in metric spaces utilizing a sample-based method. The proposed framework leverages Fr\'echet means and geodesic distances between elements in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space to create a nonparametric density model. The method's parameters are learned by minimizing the squared distances between the estimated densities and the samples. Theoretical analysis of the convergence rate is provided, along with a derivation of the general form of the loss function. The proposed framework is demonstrated through applications in time series analysis, including evaluating the normality of time series and identifying outliers.

The transition to a low-carbon economy heavily relies on decarbonization of electric power systems through increased renewable energy sources. Expanding these systems increases vulnerability to power disruptions and extreme weather events. To address these issues, a new approach to modeling and controlling complex power systems is needed, particularly at higher spatial resolutions. Developing a control framework for these systems requires a deeper understanding of their dynamics. This paper presents a new modeling approach for hierarchical power systems based on a wavelet-based method, which captures the spatial and temporal characteristics of these systems. The proposed model is then used to design a decentralized control framework that can efficiently handle large-scale power systems. This framework is tested using a high-resolution model of the US Western Interconnect, which demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed model in accurately capturing the dynamics of the actual system.

We have developed a novel approach to studying two-dimensional percolation by
combining a semi-analytical and a numerical method. This hybrid method is
designed to precisely calculate the probability of the percolating cluster at
finite sizes and in the thermodynamic limit. Our approach is based on a
combination of a semi-analytical method and a numerical method, where the
latter serves to correct the former for use in the thermodynamic limit. Our
method is demonstrated using a percolation model of a monomer-dimer lattice
system, where monomers and dummies interact via an attractive potential. Our
results show that the percolating cluster is composed of monomers, and we have
derived an analytical expression for the probability of the percolating cluster
at finite sizes. This expression is then used to correct the numerical method for
the thermodynamic limit. Our approach is also shown to be applicable to a
two-dimensional lattice percolation model, where the results reveal that the
probability of the percolating cluster is independent of the lattice structure.

Achieving uniform temperature distribution within catalytic fixed bed reactors is crucial for maintaining high performance, preventing deactivation, and ensuring overall system efficiency. However, temperature variations can occur due to factors like uneven gas flow, varying particle properties, and the impact of external factors such as weather conditions. To address this issue, this study presents a novel control strategy for correcting temperature deviations in fixed bed reactors. The proposed method utilizes a model predictive control (MPC) approach, which relies on a simplified model of the reactor to predict temperature responses and make informed control decisions. The simplified model is derived from a comprehensive 3D CFD model of the reactor, which accounts for factors like heat transfer, mass diffusion, and gas flow. By comparing the simplified and comprehensive models, their accuracy and applicability can be assessed. The proposed MPC control strategy is expected to enhance reactor performance, reduce temperature fluctuations, and minimize energy consumption.

The magnetic field map of the superconducting compound $\mathrm{Re}_2\mathrm{Hf}_2$, where superconductivity reappears at 0.8 T, is an interesting phenomenon. This reappearance of superconductivity is unusual and suggests the presence of a field-induced superconducting state. Our research, utilizing muon spin rotation/relaxation ($\mu$SR$)$ measurements under magnetic fields up to 8 T, indicate that the field-induced superconductivity is likely caused by a change in the superconducting state's symmetry. This is supported by the observation of a change in the $\mu$SR$)$ precession pattern and the detection of a second, much smaller second harmonic in the precession frequency.

In the realm of ultra-wideband (UWB) communication, a significant challenge arises from the need to manage interference and maintain reliable data transfer. To address this, researchers have developed a deep Q-learning approach to optimize UWB networks and enhance overall performance. By leveraging Q-learning to dynamically allocate UWB channels for new devices, the proposed method can effectively mitigate the impact of interference and improve network efficiency. Through extensive simulations, the researchers demonstrate that this deep Q-learning strategy yields substantial gains in terms of packet reception rate (PRR) and reduces energy consumption by up to 50% compared to conventional methods.

We investigated the $k$-median clustering problem within the realm of Hausdorff distance within a metric space. Our research revealed that this issue is generally computationally intractable. However, we found that it becomes solvable within acceptable limits of time when the space in question adheres to a specific geometric structure known as H\"{o}lder. Additionally, we discovered that a particular type of H\"{o}lder space, referred to as Riemannian, allows for an efficient solution to the $k$-median clustering problem.

Reinforcement learning for multiple agents is a complex problem compared to single-agent reinforcement learning, as it involves understanding how individual agents adapt to a shared environment from their unique perspectives. To address this challenge, researchers have developed a novel approach to multi-agent reinforcement learning, based on a model that simulates the behavior of multiple agents in a given environment. This model predicts how individual agents will adapt to the environment in the future, allowing it to make more accurate predictions of the environment than traditional reinforcement learning methods. By using this model to guide its policy, the approach can achieve superior performance on a range of benchmark tasks.

We establish a lower bound on the complexity of checking satisfiability for the least fixpoint logic LFP with equality, demonstrating that it cannot be done in polynomial time. To achieve this, we first translate LFP with equality into a fragment of least fixpoint logic that can be expressed in first-order logic with a bounded number of least fixpoints. We then show that checking satisfiability for this logic is equivalent to checking satisfiability of a specific first-order logic formula. Using a known lower bound on the complexity of first-order logic, we obtain an exponential-time upper bound on the satisfiability checking of LFP with equality.

We introduce a novel Bayesian approach to signal recovery, grounded in the
Basis Expansion Model, where the coefficients and basis functions are modeled as
random variables. The model's parameters, including the coefficients' variance
and the basis matrix, are estimated from the data. The model's flexibility
enables the use of various sparsity-inducing priors over coefficients, as well
as the incorporation of informative priors for the basis matrix. The model's
Bayesian formulation facilitates the use of Markov Chain Monte Carlo sampling,
resulting in a fully probabilistic solution. The model's effectiveness is
demonstrated through a series of numerical experiments, showcasing its ability to
recover sparse solutions in images and signals.

Air pollution poses a significant health risk worldwide, prompting a need for continuous air quality monitoring. The 'drive by sensing' approach allows for the capture of air quality data through mobile devices as they travel through urban areas. This study presents a machine learning-based system that utilizes a dataset of air quality readings from buses in London to develop a city-wide monitoring network. The network consists of 31 monitoring points, with associated buffer zones, enabling the tracking of air pollutant changes within and outside urban areas. The research then applies machine learning models to predict the air quality in the buffer zones based on the central station's readings. The study compares the performance of three machine learning algorithms - Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, and Multi-Layer Perceptron - and evaluates the impact of sampling frequency and buffer zone size on the model's accuracy. The study's findings show that the drive by sensing approach can be an effective solution for monitoring air quality in urban areas, particularly in environments with high traffic congestion.

We establish a complex Weil representation for the generalized special linear group $G$, utilizing its decomposition as a semidirect product between a unipotent radical and a finite subgroup of the general linear group. This representation is then applied to investigate properties of $G$'s maximal torus and characters.

Persuasive content creation is a highly complex and labor-intensive process that can be significantly accelerated through the use of advanced artificial intelligence. This research proposes a novel approach to generating AI-driven persuasive videos by leveraging a user-friendly, template-based framework. The process is divided into three critical stages: extracting relevant information, developing a persuasive argument, and integrating this argument with a selected video. This study contributes to the field of persuasive video generation by introducing a novel argument generation model, which utilizes a transformer-based architecture, and demonstrates the effectiveness of the approach through a comprehensive evaluation using a publicly available dataset. The results show that the model outperforms existing baselines and demonstrates robust generalization capabilities.

We introduce a novel approach to simulate the dynamics of trapped ions by employing the time-dependent variational principle (TDVP). This method is incorporated into the QuTiP framework, a widely used quantum dynamics simulator. To validate its effectiveness, we apply the method to a series of established models, including a two-level system, the harmonic oscillator, and a qubit coupled to a resonant cavity. We then utilize the approach to model a system of two ions trapped in a RF potential and interacting through laser-driven electric and magnetic forces. This system is analyzed within the TDVP approximation of infinite mass, which allows the two ions to be treated as stationary traps for a third ion. We also explore the dynamic behavior of the system and its response to external driving forces.

The rapid growth of high-performance computing capabilities has enabled researchers to thoroughly explore vast areas of uncharted parameter space within various scientific and engineering disciplines. This is particularly pertinent in the field of computational neuroscience, where complex biophysical models are often computationally intensive. By leveraging a high-performance computing infrastructure, scientists can efficiently navigate large-scale parameter spaces, identify optimal model parameters, and conduct in-depth analysis of simulated neural network behavior.

Research into camouflaged instance segmentation has been gaining momentum, but current datasets are limited in their ability to accurately represent real-world scenarios. This limitation hinders the development of effective algorithms. To address this issue, we have created a new dataset, CAMO+++, which includes a substantial number of high-quality camouflaged instances and accurate labels. This dataset offers a more comprehensive and realistic set of samples compared to existing datasets. To facilitate research, we have made the CAMO+++ dataset publicly available along with a baseline evaluation framework.

A superconducting condensate's response to a Lorentz-violating background is investigated, revealing that this violation affects the energy gap, leading to two distinct types of energy-dependent gap functions. Consequently, two related London penetration depths emerge, with one being dependent on frequency.

The development of end-user descriptions in AI models is crucial for understanding the logic behind the model's predictions and making informed decisions. However, the creation of these descriptions is a notoriously difficult task, with a lack of understanding on how to generate them. In this research, we investigate the possibility of using end-user descriptions as a tool to uncover systematic failures in AI models. A new method is proposed to create these descriptions, which is then tested on a large-scale dataset of AI model predictions. The results show that these descriptions can effectively pinpoint systematic failures in AI models and provide valuable insights into their limitations.

In object detection, a decision-making process is crucial in identifying potential objects within images. Current object detection models typically focus solely on classification, disregarding the importance of localization in making decisions. This paper introduces a novel decision-making approach that integrates localization and classification, and is adaptable to various object detection systems. Through a comprehensive evaluation on the MS COCO dataset, our approach significantly outperforms the existing decision head, enhancing decision accuracy and reducing false alarms in object detection.

Recent research has highlighted the vulnerability of deep neural networks to adversarial attacks, prompting the development of robust adversarial training methods. However, standard approaches to adversarial training have been hindered by the problem of catastrophic overfitting, which arises due to the immense diversity of possible adversarial perturbations. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a novel method of adversarial training that leverages a unique type of adversarial attack known as the soft gradient perturbation. By utilizing a combination of soft gradient perturbations and a loss function that minimizes the maximum norm of the resulting adversarial examples, we can effectively reduce the threat of catastrophic overfitting. Our approach is particularly efficient and can be easily integrated into existing adversarial training methods, as demonstrated through a comprehensive evaluation of its efficacy on the CIFAR-10 and ImageNet datasets.

This study delves into the properties of Thakurta black holes, which form due to the collision of compact objects within the context of general relativity. The research focuses on black hole formation from the merger of binary neutron stars and identifies the necessary conditions for forming a Thakurta black hole, including a specific mass limit and a limited total angular momentum. The study further examines the characteristics of Thakurta black holes, such as their event horizons, and explores the possibility of Thakurta or near-Thakurta black hole formation in the universe.

We examine the convergence properties of a broad class of zero-order, continuous-time optimization algorithms that iteratively solve complex objective functions composed of smooth, convex terms. This analysis encompasses various objective compositions, including convex functions, quadratic terms, and other regularized components. We investigate the convergence of these algorithms under two distinct scenarios: when objectives remain fixed, and when they change persistently. Under the latter case, we demonstrate that convergence is possible to a stationary point, provided objectives change at least every $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-1})$ time units. This finding is demonstrated through the application to a diverse set of problems, such as quadratic programs, compressed sensing, and matrix factorization.

A key benefit of homomorphic encryption (HE) is its ability to perform computations on encrypted data without exposure of the underlying data's details. However, the computational costs associated with these operations are substantial. To mitigate these costs, the use of key aggregation and bootstrapping has been proposed, with the latter being particularly crucial for practical deployment of HE schemes. However, bootstrapping is a resource-intensive process, making it a potential single point of failure for secure computation systems. To address this vulnerability, we propose a novel technique for parallelizing the bootstrap protocol, enabling it to be executed concurrently while maintaining correctness. We also introduce a new approach to optimizing the first homomorphic encryption application, leveraging the properties of the application to reduce the number of required bootstrap operations. By combining these two innovations, we can minimize the number of parallel bootstrap tasks needed and optimize resource allocation for secure computation systems.

We examine a class of random matrices with rotational symmetry, characterized by a confining potential of the form $V(r)=-\log r, $ yielding a semi-circle law for their eigenvalue density. This ensemble is applicable to a wide range of physical systems, including those with zero-range interactions and specific superconductivity models. We derive the joint eigenvalue distribution and density for this ensemble and apply them to a model of zero-range interacting fermions in a harmonic trap. We calculate the single-particle Green's function and use it to determine the number of fermions within the trap, along with the average and standard deviation of their density.

High-dimensional quantum systems have the potential to go beyond entanglement and explore novel forms of quantum connections, including non-entangled quantum correlations. We investigated a complex network of hypernodes, each with multiple quantum states, and interconnected qutrits, and found that these systems can exhibit unique non-local properties. Specifically, our research shows that these systems can display non-locality that cannot be explained by local hidden states, and this effect is robust against noise. Our findings open up new possibilities for understanding and exploring the non-local aspects of high-dimensional quantum systems.

Bell's theorem is often seen as the outcome of a broader conflict between causality and non-locality. Specifically, the theorem highlights the incompatibility between local causality and the principle of factorizability. However, the relationship between causality and locality is more complex, as certain approaches suggest causality aligns with locality, while others imply the two concepts may be distinct. This paper explores the relationship between local causality and factorizability, demonstrating that the former does not necessarily imply the latter. Consequently, the argument that Bell's theorem is a result of local causality failing to imply factorizability is established, thereby resolving a longstanding debate.

This study introduces a novel method for learning a dynamic video representation, 
capturing intricate temporal details and spatial correlations. Diverging from 
conventional discrete video synthesis approaches, our approach generates frames 
continuously, allowing for the efficient creation of any frame within a produced 
video. Our model is trained to predict a sequence of 3D motion vectors, 
representing an entire video, and a static camera matrix. Our results demonstrate 
the superiority of our approach over existing methods in both quality and diversity, 
as evaluated on multiple datasets. Moreover, we showcase the utility of our video 
representation in real-time video manipulation, such as frame interpolation and 
extrapolation.

We establish the geometric structure of the $\theta$-lift for the Dirac operator in a pair of dual groups, specifically focusing on the $\theta$-corresponding Dirac modules. Utilizing this framework, we demonstrate that the set of Dirac modules related to the trivial character under the $\theta$-correspondence forms a group within the set of all Dirac modules, which is then proven to be a Lie group by verifying it satisfies the necessary properties.

A novel method of measuring exposure to ionizing radiation through thermoluminescence dosimetry is reviewed in this paper. The method's principles are examined, along with its potential applications and the challenges of accurately quantifying dose rates. Various approaches to addressing these dosimetry challenges are reviewed, and their effectiveness in obtaining accurate dose measurements using thermoluminescence dosimetry is assessed.

This paper investigates a type of double phase problem under specified conditions for potential and non-linear terms, which involve a parameter that leads to loss of smoothness. To address this challenge, we combine the degree theory for operators with a truncated problem approach, along with a new cut-off technique for the pre-processed function.

A novel detector for computed tomography (CT) imaging has been developed using a high-resolution, active matrix direct electron detector designed for electron microscopy. The custom-built detector offers 1024 x 1024 pixels with a minimum detectable energy threshold of 2 keV, achieved through a compact and lightweight design. The detector's performance was evaluated through CT scans of a phantom, demonstrating the system's capability to produce 3D images with 1024 x 1024 pixels and 10 frames per second. The contrast to noise ratio (CNR) of the reconstructed images was found to be 1.5 dB, significantly outperforming a commercial CT detector.

The widespread adoption of machine learning (ML) models has led to a growing interest in post-hoc explanation techniques, aiming to provide insights into how these models operate. Despite their potential benefits, such explanations are often misused due to a lack of understanding of their limitations. This study focuses on the most advanced explanation methods, highlighting their drawbacks and potential risks of misinterpretation. The research identifies three critical concerns: (1) the inherent randomness of these methods can lead to varying results, (2) explanations may focus on the wrong aspects of ML models, and (3) the lack of transparency in how these methods work can undermine trust in them. The study concludes by emphasizing the need for rigorous evaluation, further research into post-hoc explanation techniques, and increased scrutiny of their application in practice.

Deep neural networks are increasingly being used in high-risk applications, necessitating clear and understandable predictions, which can be achieved through the field of explainable artificial intelligence. However, existing explanation methods have limitations, including a lack of generalizability and the need for retraining when network weights change, which can be addressed by utilizing a specific type of neural network called neural networks with sparse connectivity.

The presence of a singlet ground state is ruled out, and experiments indicate that the lowest-energy magnetic state is a nonmagnetic doublet. The temperature dependence of the Raman scattering of TbInO$_3$ shows a notable increase in intensity below 35 K, suggesting a change in the magnetic state. Theoretical models suggest that the magnetic state is a ferromagnetic singlet, and the presence of a nonmagnetic doublet is not ruled out. We establish the existence of ancient convex solutions, denoted as $W$-ancient solutions, in the power-of-mean curvature flow when the curvature power, $p$, exceeds $1/2$. This is achieved by modifying the rescaling method initially proposed by E. B. Bedouta and A. M. Ivochkina. The solutions, $W$, exhibit a unique property: they are either flat or have a non-zero angular bisector. Consequently, we are able to derive a lower bound for the curvature of a compact, one-dimensional manifold, denoted as $M$, as it evolves over time, $t$. This is expressed as: $$\min_{\Gamma\subset M}|\nabla N|^{2}\geq C\exp\left(-\frac{c}{(t^{\frac{p}{p-1}}-1)}\right), $$ where $N$ denotes the unit normal vector to $M$, and $C$ and $c$ are positive constants.

This paper introduces a novel technique to optimize the element-wise multiplication layer in convolutional neural networks, transforming the complex computation process into a simpler arithmetic operation in the frequency domain. The proposed algorithm leverages a combination of FFT and IFFT operations, along with local data reuse to enhance efficiency. Implemented on a high-end GPU, the optimized implementation delivers exceptional performance, achieving a remarkable speedup of up to 17 times the original rate, while also demonstrating excellent scalability on multi-GPU systems.

Our proposed deep clustering technique, known as Deep Spectral Hashing (DSH), utilizes a neural network to create a multi-layer representation of input data. DSH then applies a spectral re-encoding method to the learned representation, resulting in a high-quality clustering outcome. The approach offers several benefits, including the ability to leverage the strengths of deep learning and spectral clustering methods. The DSH technique is also efficient, scalable, and applicable to large datasets, making it a suitable solution for big data clustering challenges. Through experimental evaluation, we demonstrate the superior performance of DSH in comparison to other state-of-the-art methods.

A crucial component of risk management is accurately identifying potential risks, which is often overlooked in organizations due to a lack of suitable technology. This research aims to address this issue by developing a machine learning-based framework for risk identification, which can be integrated into existing enterprise resource planning systems. The proposed system includes a unique risk identification ontology and a user-friendly interface, and its effectiveness was evaluated through a pilot with a large financial institution.

Topological Data Analysis's innovative methods enable the discovery of hidden patterns within complex datasets through the application of various geometric approaches. This paper presents an approach to categorize datasets based on the similarity of their topological features. By analyzing the persistent homology of these features, a unique topological signature is generated for each dataset, serving as a distinct class representative. This signature is then utilized to classify future, unseen datasets. The proposed method is evaluated using two diverse datasets: a simple, handcrafted dataset and a more complex, real-world dataset derived from the MNIST handwritten digit dataset.

We investigate the connection between two process equivalence concepts, contrasimilarity and bisimilarity within a probabilistic, multi-path system model. Initially, we demonstrate that these two concepts are interchangeable within a specific, general framework. Next, we examine the implications of this relationship in two distinct, probabilistic settings. In one scenario, we find that the equivalence between contrasimilarity and bisimilarity relies on a specific probabilistic condition, whereas in the other, setting these two concepts equal results in an unexpected, unexplored consequence.

We represent the string 2-group within a 3-dimensional vector space that consists of the frame bundle over string manifolds and the associated co-bundle of strings within this frame bundle. This provides a detailed description of the string 2-group, which is analogous to De Witt's Einstein equation formulation. Furthermore, we establish a connection between the string 2-group and the unitary 2-group.

A comprehensive theoretical analysis of ion-acoustic waves and their modulational instability in non-uniform plasmas is provided, with consideration of electron-positon pairs and non-adiabatic charges. The study examines how varying plasma parameters influence wave amplitude modulation and rogue wave formation. Numerical simulations of ion-acoustic waves in laboratory plasmas reveal the presence of modulational instability and rogue waves. The research also explores the impact of electron-positron pairs and non-adiabatic charges on wave amplitude and their characteristics. Theoretical and numerical findings are compared and validated against laboratory measurements of ion-acoustic waves in plasma devices.

The behavior of Alfvén waves within a plasma is crucial for understanding the solar atmosphere's heating and the solar wind's acceleration. These waves can be categorized into two primary types: fast and slow modes, which are both compressible and have distinct polarization properties. This study focuses on non-linear interactions between these modes using a theoretical framework that considers a homogeneous, unforced plasma with a magnetic field. The investigation reveals that the generation of third-order Alfvén waves occurs through a non-linear process, which also yields an equation for their amplitude. The study further examines the energy exchange between the involved waves and identifies the conditions necessary for energy transfer between the waves and third-order waves. The study's results are also validated using numerical simulations.

The process of ambipolar diffusion plays a significant role in the gravitational collapse of filamentary molecular clouds. This study examines the effects of ambipolar diffusion on the gravitational instability of a filamentary cloud, taking into account the effects of a magnetic field. The results show that the cloud's structure is significantly influenced by ambipolar diffusion, leading to a unique density profile that is characterized by a power-law dependence on distance from the center. The cloud's stability is also affected, with ambipolar diffusion causing the growth of gravitational instability to occur more slowly than expected. The study also finds that the cloud's stability is influenced by the strength of its magnetic field, with weaker fields leading to faster growth of instability. The results of this study have implications for the formation of dense molecular cores, particularly in the context of the In-Situ Core Formation Theory.

Our research explores how the evolution of a complex quantum system can be accelerated through repetitive measurements, a concept initially demonstrated in simpler systems. We introduce a new approach to quantum control that combines control Hamiltonians and observation operators to regulate a quantum system. We demonstrate the practical application of this framework by designing an optimal control strategy to speed up the evolution of a two-state system, and we identify the essential conditions required for the successful implementation of this approach, including the ability to precisely adjust both control Hamiltonians and observation operators.

The coherence of a quantum system heavily relies on its internal properties and how they interact. In this study, we investigated the coherence of a two-spin system with Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya and anisotropic exchange interactions. We found that quantum coherence is highly direction-dependent and can be influenced by external magnetic fields. Additionally, we observed that certain types of coherence can be completely eliminated at specific critical field strengths.

This research focuses on the real-time path planning of multiple autonomous vehicles under various dynamic conditions and tight time constraints. A novel algorithm is presented to determine an optimal route for these vehicles to reach their destinations while maintaining a predetermined safe distance, even in the face of sudden obstacles. The proposed method leverages a high-dimensional search space to efficiently find the shortest path among numerous possible routes. A comprehensive evaluation of the vehicles' dynamics and mobility limitations is also incorporated into the planning process. A range of numerical simulations are conducted to demonstrate the effectiveness of the planning approach.

Unsupervised Domain Adaptation has shown great potential in resolving challenges in autonomous driving tasks, such as lane detection, but its practical application is hindered by the domain-invariant extraction of semantic information. We propose a novel domain adaptation method for lane detection, which incorporates a spatial transformer module to selectively remove target domain noise from lane markings. This approach, which we call Target Marking Selection, leverages the effectiveness of lane marking confidence scores to identify and isolate noise from lane detection, thereby enhancing domain-invariant adaptation. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method through extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets, resulting in superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art approaches.

The interaction between a water drop and a hydrogel coated with particles is crucial in understanding the mechanisms behind self-cleaning surfaces. By employing molecular dynamics simulations, we investigated the dynamic processes involved in the cleaning process. Our findings indicate that the presence of particles on the hydrogel surface significantly influences the cleaning process. Specifically, we observed that the absorption of the water drop is delayed when particles are present, leading to a notable increase in the cleaning efficiency of the substrate. A theoretical model was developed to explain this phenomenon, which revealed that the absorption time of the water drop is influenced by the concentration of adsorbed particles. Furthermore, we found that the cleaning process is affected by the size of the hydrogel domain, leading to a decrease in efficiency with increasing domain size.

This study delves into the connection between course context and student collaboration 
through an analysis of data from the Higher Education Data Sharing (HEDS) project. By 
examining survey data from nearly 3,500 students in over 1,200 courses, the study 
uncovered a positive correlation between student collaboration and improved academic 
performance. Notably, this effect was more pronounced in larger classes and those with 
more diverse student bodies. Conversely, courses with a high representation of female 
instructors revealed a negative correlation between student collaboration and academic 
outcomes. The study's findings suggest that while increased collaboration among students 
can yield positive results, the overall impact is contingent upon various factors, 
including course size, student demographics, and instructor gender.

Radar Wind Profilers are widely used to study atmospheric dynamics due to their ability to penetrate clouds and gather detailed data. A common challenge in wind profiling is the presence of atmospheric ducts, which can cause multiple signal paths and result in inaccurate readings. This research presents a new method to separate and remove multiple reflections from raw RADAR data, which can be applied to data from any source. This approach was tested using data from a 5.5 m tall duct and a 149.8 MHz RADAR antenna, and was found to successfully separate and remove the secondary reflection. This development has significant potential for improving wind speed measurements in atmospheric ducts and may also have applications in other fields where multiple signal paths are a concern.

We have identified a previously unknown young star cluster, designated as NGC 2287, through a combination of Gaia EDR3 astrometry and near-infrared photometry from UKIDSS/LAS and 2MASS. The cluster consists of approximately 30 stars, with a notable concentration of 16 stars within a 1-degree radius of the cluster center. The cluster's center is located at approximately 06 55 14.30 +28 38 55.20, with a radius of approximately 2.5 minutes. The cluster's properties, including proper motion, parallax, and proper motion dispersion, have been determined through the application of the maximum likelihood method. The cluster's age is estimated to be around 5 million years, with a distance of approximately 1.5 kiloparsecs, and an eccentricity of nearly 0.93, indicating that it is in an elliptical shape. Incorporating synthetic translations can be a valuable resource for bilingual text mining. This study examines the feasibility of generating these synthetic translations using a single monolingual model, thereby eliminating the need for a parallel corpus. A novel approach, called "paraphrase injection," is proposed, where a transformer-based model is trained to generate paraphrases in one language, and the results are automatically translated into the other language, producing synthetic translations. Experimental results on multiple datasets reveal that the proposed method achieves comparable performance to more complex methods that utilize parallel data and additional training objectives.

The interplay between unitary and dissipative dynamics significantly affects the scaling of entanglement in various complex quantum systems. We investigated this phenomenon in a model of a large-scale quantum heat engine consisting of many qubits, which interact with their environment. By analyzing the out-of-time-order correlation, we found that the competition between thermalization and quantum many-body revivals leads to distinct phases of entanglement scaling, which are influenced by the system's temperature and heat capacity. These findings have implications for understanding the entanglement distribution in engineered quantum systems.

A novel, electric field-driven mechanism of interlayer hybridization has been discovered in transition metal dichalcogenide heterobilayers. This mechanism is unique and distinct from the traditional chemical bonding-driven hybridization. The presence of a perpendicular electric field causes the interlayer hybridization of valence band top and conduction band bottom states, leading to the creation of a non-trivial topological phase. This topological phase is characterized by a non-zero Berry curvature and a non-trivial Chern number. The effect of the electric field on the topological phase is studied through the band structure, Berry curvature, and Chern number. The study also reveals that the topological phase can be tuned by adjusting the electric field strength. The research has significant implications for the design of electric field-controlled topological quantum materials.

This research explores the echo state property within the context of quantum reservoir computing. Unlike its classical counterpart, determining the echo state property in quantum reservoir computing is significantly more challenging due to the intricate nature of quantum systems. We have derived essential criteria for the echo state property to hold true in quantum reservoir computing, utilizing a broader framework that encompasses various quantum echo state networks. Our findings are grounded in the state operator approach, which provides a unified perspective on quantum reservoir computing. We have also established a fundamental theorem outlining the necessary and sufficient conditions for the echo state property to hold in quantum reservoir computing.

We have developed a versatile hybrid circuit that combines photonic waveguides and trapped single atoms, allowing for flexible and efficient information transfer. This innovative design enables the precise alignment of laser beams to atom-based interfaces, where data is either transmitted or received. By leveraging this technology, we can create a range of quantum-based applications, including the manipulation of quantum states and the integration of quantum memories with other photonic devices.

This study presents a novel approach to solving the Laplace equation, using a combination of a random search algorithm and a unique decomposition method, which replaces traditional meshing techniques. Two novel numerical methods are proposed, both of which utilize a novel approach to solve systems of equations efficiently. The performance of these methods is evaluated and compared to traditional mesh-free and search-based approaches, with a comprehensive analysis of their strengths and weaknesses. The results show that these new methods are competitive with existing approaches, making the proposed approach a promising alternative for solving a wide range of partial differential equations, particularly those with complex geometries and multi-dimensional domains.

This study examines the interplay between dark energy and dark matter in a flat, expanding universe, with a particular focus on the effects of interacting dark energy on the stability of critical points in the phase space. We investigate the interplay between the Hubble parameter and the equation of state of dark energy, with a view to identifying the conditions under which these critical points are either stable or unstable. Our analysis reveals that, in the absence of interactions, these points are always stable. Conversely, when dark energy and dark matter interact, there are scenarios in which the interacting fixed point is either a stable node or an unstable saddle point. Notably, these points are connected by trajectories that are either stable or unstable. Our findings also show that, in the absence of interactions, certain critical points are either stable or unstable, but that these points are destroyed when dark energy and dark matter interact, with a resulting change in the stability of nearby trajectories.

The occurrence of relativistic outflows linked to optical tidal disruption events has been confirmed by the observation of radio emission. A significant challenge in studying these outflows lies in the lack of a comprehensive catalog of TDEs with extensive radio coverage. A recent study utilized the Zwicky Transient Facility to identify TDEs in the nearby local group of galaxies. The researchers discovered 14 TDEs in the host galaxies at a distance of less than 3 Gpc, which were selected based on the presence of a UV-optical flare and a UV-optical spectrum consistent with a stellar object. The team found that 6 out of 14 TDEs exhibited radio emission, with 2 of them displaying outflow characteristics. The researchers also found that the host galaxies of TDEs with radio emission have higher star formation rates than those without. The team suggests that the host galaxies of TDEs with radio emission have higher star formation rates, indicating that the accretion of material from stars may power the outflows. The researchers also found that the host galaxies of TDEs with radio emission have higher black hole masses than those without. The team suggests that the accretion of material from stars may also be responsible for the higher black hole masses.
